title: By whose grace, the body
hookLine: by His grace you have a healthy body and a home

lines: THE ROOF, THE NIGHT IT LEAKS.
BY WHOSE GRACE: BODY AND HOME.
cards: Most of us only notice our bodies when something goes wrong. A sprained ankle, and every step is a project. A cold, and you'd give anything for one clear breath through the nose.
Then it heals, and within a week you've forgotten again. The same with home: you notice the roof the night it leaks.
Ashtpadi six keeps saying jih prasaad, by whose grace, and in its later stanzas it turns to the two things we forget most completely: the body we live in, and the house that holds it.

teach.b: One line says: jih prasaad aarog kanchan dehee. By whose grace you have a healthy, golden body. Aarog is health, being free of illness.
Dehee is the body. A golden body isn't about looks: in the old poetry, gold is what's precious and doesn't tarnish. The second half, as always, turns: attune yourself to that loving Lord.

teach.h: A HOUSE, A FAMILY, HONOR KEPT.
teach.b: The same ashtpadi has already spoken of the house: by whose grace you live in a mansion of comfort, by whose grace you dwell at peace with your family.
Another line says, by whose grace your honor is kept covered: the things you'd rather nobody saw, quietly protected. Put those together and you get an ordinary good day.
You woke up, you could move, nobody embarrassed you, there was a door to close behind you and people inside it.
The stanza says none of that is automatic. Each is a jih prasaad.
This doesn't mean anyone who is ill, or without a home, has lost grace.

Gurbani speaks of rich and poor, healthy and sick, as living within the same hukam, and Sikhs are asked to share what they have, which is why the langar, the gurdwara kitchen, serves a free meal to anyone who comes in.
The stanza speaks to the one who has these things and forgets them, and asks that person to notice.

how: Sikhs read the 'jih prasaad' stanzas of Sukhmani Sahib as reminders that health, home and family are gifts, and many share what they have through langar and seva.

o: a home where a family lives in peace
the body, a precious gift of grace
the soul that lives on after death

games.q: the body and the home — tap the pairs.

s: a 'golden body' in the stanza is about good looks
gold means precious and untarnished: a healthy, working body.
the stanza says the sick or homeless have lost grace
it speaks to the one who has these gifts and forgets them.
ashtpadi six also gives thanks for living at peace with family
by whose grace you dwell at peace with your family.

games.q: your sprained ankle has healed. a week later, by ashtpadi six, what's the move?
o: notice the healthy body as a gift, by whose grace.
games.why: jih prasaad aarog kanchan dehee: by whose grace this healthy, precious body, and the stanza turns you toward the Giver.

practice: Start at your feet, which carried you today, then your hands, which held things, then your lungs, breathing all by themselves; whatever hurts, let it be there too, you're not pretending.

Then widen out to the room, the walls, the roof, whoever shares this home with you, or the quiet if no one does. If you pray, give thanks with the words jih prasaad; if you don't, let each part simply be noticed and valued.

wordCard.voice: Dehee, the body. By whose grace a healthy, precious body, and a home to live in.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: dehee, the body; in ashtpadi six, the 'golden body' given by grace.

carryVoice: Your line: by his grace, this home. A roof, a door, and people inside it. See you tomorrow.

sources.work: Guru Granth Sahib (Guru Arjan, Gauri Sukhmani)
